text.title: Nasdaq's 4.5% plunge fades as Dow erases 1,100-point loss; AI selloff and tariffs keep nerves high
text.summary: US stocks staged a sharp intraday recovery but finished split: the Dow rose 0.3% and the Russell 2000 gained 0.7%, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.3% and the Nasdaq fell 0.6%. The Nasdaq had been down as much as 4.5% earlier in the session. Treasuries rallied, with the 10-year yield down 5 bp to 4.85%, and the dollar eased 0.1%. Oil jumped 2.5% to $84.12 and gold edged up 0.5%. The thread is a continuing unwind in the AI trade, layered with new tariff proposals and sticky inflation data. Money moved out of the most crowded tech names and into cyclicals and defensives, and the VIX rose 7.3% to 28.3.
text.rates: The 10-year yield fell 5 bp to 4.85%, and the 2-year fell 2 bp to 4.61%. The 10-year is down 22 bp over five days and 31 bp below its one-month high. The dollar index slipped 0.1% to 103.7 as early strength after the data faded. Oil rose 2.5% to $84.12, though the headlines do not explain the jump, and energy shares gained 0.7%. Gold rose 0.5% to $3,608 after CNBC said it touched a more-than-one-year low earlier in the session on the inflation data. Lower yields normally help long-duration growth stocks, but safe-haven buying and the AI unwind outweighed that for tech.
text.breadth: Leadership was broad and cyclical-leaning beneath the index headlines. Materials, real estate, communication services, industrials, financials, energy, utilities and staples all rose, while technology (-0.8%), health care (-0.6%) and consumer discretionary (-0.2%) lagged. The Russell 2000 and Dow outperformed the Nasdaq. This looks like rotation out of crowded AI leaders rather than a wholesale retreat from risk. The VIX at 28.3 is still elevated, up 53.8% over one month.
text.context: The S&P 500 has now fallen two straight sessions and is down 1.9% over five days and 6.4% over one month, 7.3% below its one-month high. The Nasdaq is 11.2% below its high. J.P. Morgan's weekly recap notes the week through Nov 20 was steeply negative, with the S&P 500 down 8.6%, technology down 12.1% and large-cap growth lagging large-cap value. Per that recap, large-cap growth is down 13.6% year-to-date while large-cap value is up 18.9%.
text.takeaway: Sharp intraday reversals like today's are a reminder that volatility can be large in both directions, and that single-day moves say little about longer-term outcomes. Diversification across sectors, styles and asset classes is designed for periods when leadership shifts quickly.
text.talk: Markets were very volatile today. The Nasdaq was down more than 4% at one point before a strong recovery, as concerns about AI stocks and new tariff proposals continued to weigh on sentiment. Over the past few weeks, though, the broader market has pulled back, and longer-term investors are typically served by staying diversified.

drivers.t: The Nasdaq plunged as much as 4.5% before paring losses, and the WSJ described a market struggling to find its footing in the new AI trade. Nvidia was a focal point. MarketWatch, citing Vanda Research, said it has given back more than half of Monday's rally and that retail dip-buyers' recent gains are nearly gone. Rich growth valuations are most sensitive to shifts in sentiment, so a failed bounce in a market leader tends to spread to the wider tech complex. Technology fell 0.8% on the day, the weakest of the major sectors besides health care.

The WSJ tied the tech giveback to gains made after Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. Separately, Vance said he was assured Huang was not under DOJ investigation, and Reuters reported how the administration concluded Huang is not a national security threat. The headlines do not link these developments to the day's price action, so the effect on Nvidia shares is unclear. They do show how much headline risk is attached to the sector's largest names.

The US proposed surprise new tariffs on Brazilian imports, including a 10% duty on aircraft. Bloomberg reported the rates also raise the stakes for India to reach a trade deal or face a higher levy, leaving exporters with little clarity. Reuters said the tariff turmoil added to tech pain for volatility-weary investors. Tariffs tend to raise input costs and cloud earnings visibility, which pushes investors toward safer assets and lifts volatility measures.

Treasury yields fell after a flurry of data that included the PCE price index. CNBC said investors bought bonds for protection even as inflation proved sticky. Reuters also reported Fed policymakers are at odds over the causes of high inflation. Falling yields on a day like this reflect demand for safety more than optimism about growth. The 10-year ended 5 bp lower at 4.85% and the 2-year 2 bp lower at 4.61%.

The Dow closed higher after wiping out a 1,100-point loss, and Bloomberg noted markets staged a dramatic recovery. Materials led the S&P sectors at +2.1%, followed by real estate at +0.9%, communication services at +0.9% and industrials at +0.8%. Financials rose 0.7% and energy 0.7%. The headlines do not explain the materials surge. Small caps outperformed, with the Russell 2000 up 0.7%, which suggests dip-buying outside of mega-cap tech.

Bloomberg reported GTCR is weighing a roughly $50B buyout of Global Payments, which would be one of the largest leveraged buyouts ever. Targa is reportedly in talks to buy Kinetik. Sanofi shares hit their highest since May 2025 following its planned $41B Insmed acquisition. A Paul Weiss M&A chair spoke of a record pace for M&A and said the volatility is unlikely to continue. Strong dealmaking suggests corporate and private-equity buyers still see value after the selloff.

earnings.t: MarketWatch called HP's beat 'low-quality' but said it was still enough to make the stock a standout gainer in the tech rout. Investors are still rewarding earnings beats even in a weak tape.
